model_vs_baselines.verdict_text: At a 25% contact cap, the model's top customers gave 10.0 additional buyers per 1,000 Mens e-mails (95% interval 2.8 to 17.2), against 7.4 for random contacts (difference +2.6, interval -3.5 to 8.7) and 8.6 for the recency rule (difference +1.4, interval -5.5 to 8.2). The model is ahead on the point estimate, but both intervals must exclude zero for a stable gain and they do not: no stable targeting gain is shown. The past-spend rule, which validation did not select as the primary rule, scored 11.6 (model minus that rule -1.6, interval -7.0 to 3.9).

recommendation.decision: Send the Mens e-mail to every eligible, consented existing customer except a 10% randomized no-e-mail holdout, but only after finance and CRM confirm that the full cost per e-mail is below the break-even for the confirmed margin. Do not use the targeting model to exclude customers yet. A named human approves; this system sends nothing.
conditions: Finance confirms the contribution margin on incremental sales and CRM confirms the full cost per e-mail (delivery, offer, handling); the cost must be below margin x 0.77 USD, and below margin x 0.49 USD to be safe on the lower bound.
E-mail consent and unsubscribe handling are verified for every recipient.
A 10% randomized no-e-mail holdout is drawn and frozen before sending (at least 3,063 customers per arm to detect an effect of the 2008 size with 80% power).
A named human approves the final draft; any change to the plan requires a new review.
The 2008 effect is a prior, not a forecast: the first send is itself the pilot and is judged on its own holdout.
rationale: Randomized evidence on 64,000 existing customers: 267 of 21,307 customers bought within two weeks after the Mens e-mail (1.25%) against 122 of 21,306 with no e-mail (0.57%).
That is 6.8 additional purchasing customers per 1,000 e-mailed (95% interval 5.0 to 8.6). The Womens e-mail added 3.1 per 1,000 (interval 1.5 to 4.7) against the same control.
On the held-out test split the Mens e-mail sent to everyone added 7.4 per 1,000 (interval 4.6 to 10.3), consistent with the full sample.

At a 25% contact cap, the model's top customers gave 10.0 additional buyers per 1,000 Mens e-mails (95% interval 2.8 to 17.2), against 7.4 for random contacts (difference +2.6, interval -3.5 to 8.7) and 8.6 for the recency rule (difference +1.4, interval -5.5 to 8.2). The model is ahead on the point estimate, but both intervals must exclude zero for a stable gain and they do not: no stable targeting gain is shown. The past-spend rule, which validation did not select as the primary rule, scored 11.6 (model minus that rule -1.6, interval -7.0 to 3.9).

Incremental spend is 0.77 USD per customer e-mailed (interval 0.49 to 1.05). Margin and cost per e-mail are UNKNOWN, so no profit is claimed; at an assumed 35% margin the e-mail may cost up to 0.27 USD (0.17 USD on the lower bound) before it loses money, setup aside.
would_reverse_if: Verified cost per e-mail above the break-even for the verified margin (point: margin x 0.77 USD): choose no e-mail.
Consent cannot be verified, or unsubscribe and complaint costs are material: choose no e-mail or a smaller consented group.
A new randomized pilot on the current base gives an interval for additional buyers that includes zero: stop and research before spending more.
A larger test shows the model beating random and the simple rule with intervals above zero: switch to model-targeted sending.
A binding contact cap (budget or frequency policy): prioritise by a simple auditable rule and randomize inside the cap, as described in the alternative.
recommendation.alternative_if_model_inconclusive: If only a share of customers may be contacted, do not present the model as a proven gain. At a 25% cap the model (10.0), the recency rule (8.6) and the past-spend rule (11.6) all sit above random (7.4) on the point estimate, none with an interval that excludes zero. Use the simplest auditable ranking (past-year spend or recency) to fill the cap, and randomize e-mail versus no e-mail inside both the selected and the unselected group, so the next campaign measures whether targeting works.
recommendation.no_email_option: Always allowed. Without an e-mail 0.57% of customers still bought within two weeks; those purchases are not caused by the campaign. Choose no e-mail when cost per contact exceeds break-even, when consent is missing, or when a manager prefers to wait for a current pilot. Under the conservative assumption set the Womens e-mail loses money (-2,871 USD scenario contribution).

holdout_plan.primary_metric: unique purchasing customers within two weeks, treated minus holdout

marketing.research_question: Among existing customers who bought in the past twelve months, does a merchandise e-mail create additional purchasing customers within two weeks compared with no e-mail, which of the two e-mails does it better, and is a targeting model worth using under a contact cap?
marketing.audience: Existing customers who purchased in the past twelve months (64,000 in the experiment). This is repeat-purchase stimulation of a known base, not acquisition of new customers.
marketing.segmentation: Bases available before the e-mail: months since last purchase, past-year spend, past-year purchase category (Mens, Womens or both; product history, not gender), new-in-the-past-year flag, zip type and purchase channel. Descriptive only, by past-year category: Mens e-mail: Mens merchandise only: 6.0 per 1,000 (interval 3.4 to 8.6); Womens merchandise only: 5.7 per 1,000 (interval 3.2 to 8.2); Both: 15.0 per 1,000 (interval 7.4 to 22.6). Womens e-mail: Mens merchandise only: 0.6 per 1,000 (interval -1.5 to 2.8); Womens merchandise only: 5.1 per 1,000 (interval 2.6 to 7.6); Both: 5.3 per 1,000 (interval -1.2 to 11.9).
marketing.targeting: Default target: every eligible, consented customer except the randomized holdout. The Mens e-mail added buyers in all three purchase categories; the Womens e-mail shows a clear effect only among customers who bought Womens merchandise. The model's ranking is not shown to beat random or a simple rule with a stable margin, so it is not used to suppress anyone.
marketing.positioning: For customers who bought from us this year: a timely reminder of new merchandise from a retailer they already know, giving a reason to return within two weeks. Lead with the Mens e-mail focus because it produced more additional buyers. Copy is a hypothesis: the 2008 creative is not available.

alternatives: Womens e-mail: 3.1 additional buyers per 1,000 (interval 1.5 to 4.7)
four_ps.note: Product here means the merchandise focus of the e-mail. The dataset has no SKU, assortment or stock data.

four_ps.decision: No price or discount change is recommended.
alternatives: Test a plain reminder against an offer in the next randomized pilot
four_ps.note: Price and discount terms of the 2008 e-mails are unknown; any offer cost belongs in cost per contact.

four_ps.decision: E-mail to existing customers, compared with no contact.
alternatives: Other channels: not tested in this experiment
four_ps.note: The customer's past purchase channel (phone, web, multichannel) is a feature, not the campaign channel.

four_ps.decision: Two draft messages prepared as hypotheses; a human approves or rejects them.
alternatives: Merchandise-matched variant for Womens-category buyers, to be tested rather than assumed
four_ps.note: The actual creative, subject line and products shown in 2008 are not available. Drafts are never sent by this system.

journey_barrier_hypotheses: UNVERIFIED: recent buyers have no trigger to return within two weeks; an e-mail supplies one.

UNVERIFIED: a message about merchandise a customer has never bought is less relevant (the Womens e-mail added 0.6 per 1,000 among customers who bought only Mens merchandise; this describes a group and does not prove the reason).
UNVERIFIED: something between the visit and the purchase stops most e-mail-driven visitors; site and checkout friction are not observed in this dataset.

action_plan.action: Review the eligible segment (purchased in the past twelve months) and report its current size.
Verify e-mail consent and unsubscribe handling for every eligible customer.
Supply the contribution margin and the full cost per e-mail; compare with the break-even thresholds.
Draw and freeze a 10% randomized no-e-mail holdout before any send.
Approve or reject the draft with name, reason and plan version; re-review after any change.
Send only after step 5 is approved. This system has no send tool.
After two weeks, compare unique buyers, incremental spend, cost and unsubscribes between e-mailed customers and the holdout; decide to continue, change or stop.

marketing.success_metric: Additional unique purchasing customers per 1,000 e-mailed versus the randomized holdout within two weeks, with a 95% interval above zero. Secondary: incremental spend per contact times margin minus cost per contact. Guardrail: unsubscribe and complaint rate.

warnings: REPEATED EVALUATION: the dataset was analysed before; the test split is not untouched data.
RARE OUTCOME: 578 buyers among 64,000 customers. Top-k and subgroup cells hold few buyers, so targeting comparisons are imprecise.
GROUP EFFECTS ONLY: differences between randomized groups estimate additional repeat buyers for a population; they are not an individual's effect and not customer acquisition.
HISTORICAL: a 2008 effect for one anonymous apparel retailer. Do not transfer it to another retailer or to a current base without a new randomized pilot.
ECONOMICS ARE SCENARIOS: margin and cost per e-mail are unknown; no contribution figure is a measured profit.
No e-mail is ever sent, scheduled or approved by this system; a named human decides.
